Mr. Speaker, the motion placed before the House by my colleague, the hon. member for Oshawa, is of profound concern and of great importance to Liberal Members of Parliament as well as to the rank and file of the Liberal Party of Canada.
The substance of the motion, that is dealing with the plight of poor Canadian children, ought to be one of the highest priorities for all members of this great institution. Today, many Canadians enjoy a quality of life, a standard of living, which leaves many throughout the world envious of our socio-economic status. There are, however, certain hard realities whose consequences are inescapable. To deny that childhood poverty is not common in Canada would be totally irresponsible and factually incorrect.
I believe it important that we place on the record certain facts which are indisputable. More than 1 million Canadian children live in poverty, up 120,000 since 1980, and over 60 per cent of these children come from single female-led families who are poor.
Canada's children are poor because their parents are poor. The gap between the rich and the poor is sadly growing and growing under this administration. The poorest 40 per cent of Canadians received less of Canada's total income in 1986 than they did in 1980. At the same time, the wealthiest 40 per cent increased their share of the total income.
Poor children suffer ill health, hardship and educational failure. Twice as many poor children fall behind in school as do children from rich families. According to the National Council on Welfare, children now make up the single largest group of poor people in the country. In 1986, more than 1 million children were growing up in poverty. That is about one child in six.
The poverty rate for families headed by persons not in the labour force is approximately 23 per cent compared to 9 per cent for families in which the head of the family is doing paid work. The risk of poverty is greater for young children. Twenty-one per cent of children below the age of six and 19 per cent of those between the ages of six and 14 are growing up in poverty.
There are almost 7.5 million Canadian children under the age of 20 in Canada. In 1985, 6,000 of those children died. Of the 365,000 babies bom in Canada in 1985, nearly 3,000 died before reaching their first birthday.
A recent Canadian survey indicated that the child mortality rate is twice as high among families at the lowest income level than among those at the highest income level.
Other facts are clear, unequivocal and very disheartening. The major cause of hospitalization of children under 14 is respiratory illness. A recent Canadian study indicated that the mortality rate from respiratory illness was twice as high among boys and six times higher among girls from low-income families than among children of high-income families.
A recent study in Ontario found that being on welfare was one of the strongest predictors of psychiatric disorders and chronic health problems among children. When you review the statistics as evidenced by agencies of the Government of Canada, one is not only disconcerted with these facts but, indeed, I find them to be alarming.
Child poverty statistics on a province by province basis in 1986 show that in the province of Newfoundland, a province dear to my heart, families in excess of 44,000 were believed to be in poverty. Female single parents in that province number roughly 7,800, that being a percentage of 72.9 per cent. In Nova Scotia, my own province, 39,000 families were found to be in poverty. The female single parents in that province number roughly 15,000 for a percentage of 70.9 per cent found to be below the poverty level for children under 16 years of age.
Such families in the province of Alberta number 93,000. Female single parents number 34,000 for a percentage of 51.3. So goes the statistics which for all of us must be alarming and it deserves our careful attention and speedy action.
Let me discuss native people. In 1977, the number of hospital admissions of native Indians because of infections and parasitic diseases was about seven times higher than the national average. In 1983, the mortality rate among native infants was two times higher for Indians, four times higher for Inuit than the national rate. In 1982, the mortality rate was almost three times higher
November 24, 1989

for native children ages one to four years than for non-native children. And the facts go on.
Native Canadians are also at risk. In 1981, 50 per cent of native people were in the labour force and the average income was two-thirds less for natives than for non-natives.
I put these facts on the record, not to be disputatious with my colleagues who will speak after me, but it is an attempt to have members of Parliament focus on the true meaning of those particular facts and the consequences of them for young Canadians.
I do not speak today of bridges. I do not speak of airplanes, bricks and mortar. I speak of young Canadians who have dreams and aspirations as diverse as those of the men and women who occupy these seats in perhaps the greatest institution in the world.
The human face of poverty in our country must be described, it must be articulated, but more important, it must be felt and it requires action by those of us who now occupy positions of responsibility.
A report in my own province entitled Women and Children Last of February, 1989 talks about single mothers on welfare in the province of Nova Scotia. For the benefit of those members who are here today, I would like to read two excerpts for their edification and, indeed, for their reflection.
This is a social worker in the province of Nova Scotia commenting on a situation. I quote from page 56 of that document:
A social worker at the Izaak Walton Killam Children's Hospital has seen single mothers bringing their babies into the emergency room with diarrhea and vomiting. They tell the doctors who examine their babies that they have been feeding them diluted whole milk, or Similac diluted at twice the normal amount. Their welfare checks were insufficient to permit them to buy Similac, which is much more costly than milk, or to buy enough of it. A month's supply of Similac costs around $60. These mothers are not aware that their efforts to stretch an inadequate income have led to their babies' illnesses. "They just blanch at the thought of having to give the proper amount of Similac because of the cost."
A basic necessity of life for young children is milk. We have not only in my province but across this country individuals confronted with similar serious situations. I believe that to be horrifying for Canadians anywhere in this great country.
Supply
Page 57 of the same document talks about a child with asthma:
The medications and Medi-Mist he needs cost between $80 and $100 a month. But $80 or $100 is far beyond the means of his mother, who receives Family Benefits. The tragic consequence for this child and others like him is that he is not getting the treatment he needs. When asthma is poorly controlled, a child is much more likely to suffer from attacks of life-threatening breathlessness. Hospitalization may follow such crises. The child may have to spend approximately ten days in hospital before his asthma can be brought under control. Then the vicious cycle is likely to repeat itself a few weeks or a few months later, when once again, the child's parent is unable to afford the treatments he needs.
This again is another real life example, not some bare-faced statistic found within Statistics Canada or the National Council on Welfare. It is real people experiencing the difficulties and the necessities of trying to have a healthy and happy life.
For what it is worth, it must be frustrating for those who are out there confronted with these serious issues and the problems that they manufacture not only for poor children, but for poor families, to see that our government has reacted not in a great positive way but indeed in a negative way. There has been the partial deindexing of family allowance, the reduced turnover point for the refundable child tax credit threshold which the RCTC has decreased based on family earnings from $26,300 to $23,500, partial deindexing of this threshold level, the net effect which will be an increasing number of near-poor families losing some of that child tax credit. There has been a reduction in the child tax exemption from $710 to $390 by 1989, and a partial deindexing of this exemption. Thx reform has since reduced this exemption to a rather insignificant credit of $65.
I could go on with regard to the lack of programs in terms of child care or in terms of the proliferation of personal income taxes that have caused grief to many Canadians and particularly poor families.
The motion put forward by my colleague from Oshawa was done, I think, in an attempt to marshall and harness the spirit which is within Parliament to address this problem not only conceptually but, indeed, from an action perspective.
The causes of child poverty are great and many. Child poverty is directly related to family poverty, and families without meaningful employment and economic opportunities in this country continue to find that their plight

November 24, 1989
Supply
and the plight of their children will be directly related to those economic opportunities.
An inadequate educational and training system both at the federal and at the provincial levels is also facilitating the difficulties in terms of causing poverty and child poverty in this country. The lack of affordable, accessible and quality child care in this country again is another cause, a cause in which I believe all of us should join and try to find new child care spaces in this country.
There has also been a failure of institutions, the failure of Parliament to deal with the necessities that young poverty-stricken children will have to face, but also the failure of other institutions such as the courts which have been less than adequate, have not persevered, have not been vigorous in forcing maintenance orders upon those spouses who duly must and ought to pay those maintenance payments to families who are in need of that financial assistance.
It is an absolute disgrace that an institution such as the courts across this country, administered by the provinces, are allowing individuals to act irresponsibly and not pay the maintenance orders that a court deemed to be appropriate.
About the welfare system itself, I could tell you story upon story. I come from a riding where the poverty is real and the welfare system acts to prohibit and restrict the incentive of the individual.
In Nova Scotia, we have a system which I would deem archaic. The cross-examination and the evaluations that these people must go through in order to receive some assistance to care for their children and their families is, in many instances, unbelievable.
When you lose your dignity, you lose everything, and I would hope that as we reflect upon the substance of this motion, as we reflect upon what we can do as parliamentarians, we will look squarely and clearly at the national systems that we have in place which are very inadequate indeed in addressing the concerns of our welfare system.
Many of those individuals who work in that system are caring, compassionate, loving persons. But equally so, I am afraid to say, there are numerous individuals who have lost the compassion, the sensitivity and the understanding to deal with those problems with which they are being confronted with on a daily basis.
I recognize that my time is limited. However, I would like to close, if I may, with a quote from a book entitled Two Worlds of Childhood. It says the following which I believe to be descriptive of the substance and the spirit of the motion today and hopefully can be descriptive of the action that we as a Parliament may take:
This is the place to start, for that is where the children are. For only a hard look at the world in which they live-a world we adults have created for them in large part by default-can convince us of the urgency of their plight and the consequences of our inaction. Then perhaps it will come to pass that, in the words of Isaiah, 'A little child shall lead them."
I urge all members to support the motion to demonstrate to Canadians that Parliament, the rock of democracy, has the capacity, and, more important, the political will to confront and to resolve child poverty throughout this great nation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the hon. member's speech in the lobby and here in the House, and the Minister has said, and we will say it again today in the course of this debate, that we fully support the motion presented by the Leader of the New Democratic Party However, poverty among children is not something that came out of the blue. I may remind the hon. member that a political party and a government must have vision and look to the future.
When the Liberal government was in power, at the beginning of the quiet revolution, it was a time when families started to have problems and women were taking their place in society. At the same time, divorce, separation, and so forth, were becoming more common. And at a time when this country needed a long-term policy that would prepare for the impact of the quiet revolution on today's society, the government went off on an incredible spending spree with taxpayers' money. In my own riding, we had the expropriation of 97,000 acres for Mirabel. Millions of dollars of taxpayers' money was spent for nothing, because the government was later obliged to sell the land back to the owners.
I would like to ask the hon. member who was a member of the Liberal government for almost a quarter of a century, for 25 years, how he can-we all agree that child poverty is insidious, it is unacceptable, it does not

make sense and that everyone must do what he can to help alleviate the problem. Elowever, I wish the hon. member would explain how we can deal with child poverty if we take only a fraction of the money we need to pay the interest on the cost of servicing the debt, because that is what we are doing now. We have a national debt that has assumed incredible proportions, while at the same time, as we approach the year 2000, we must deal with the problems of sexual abuse. I am very much concerned, and the subject was brought up by the hon. member and the minister as well, and the Rix Rogers report will be submitted very shortly, and I am sure that all members will be appalled when they read that in Canada, more and more children are suffering sexual abuse, children that today need treatment because after sexual abuse something must be done. But all this takes enormous amounts of money! The last ministers' conference made it abundantly clear that the needs that exist are an administrative nightmare. So could the hon. member explain what he did when he was in the government to try and deal with this problem or to take preventive action?

Mr. Speaker, the time allowed me is sufficient to explain all of the positive things that my government was able to do in the years in which I was fortunate enough to be a representative of the people of my constituency from 1980 to 1984.1 do wish to say to the hon. member that I know she would not want us to enter into a long, winding debate of political partisanship and of pointing the blame at different individuals. However, since she has done that, it may be necessary for me to accommodate the hon. member in response to the question she raises.
There is no question that for governments at every level, Conservative, Liberal and NDP, provincially and federally, there is sufficient blame to go around. If members of Parliament want to point the finger at someone else other than themselves, that is fine, but that does nothing to eradicate the serious situation which affects young children and families in this country.
Yes, there were family allowances. Yes, we did something with regard to the Canada Assistance Act. Yes, we
Supply
did many things with regard to the child tax credit. A whole host of things took place with regard to trying to address some of those issues.
But I say to the hon. member that that ought not to be the question. The question that she poses is: Where is the money? Where is the money going to come from in addressing this most serious situation? I suggest to the hon. member that one must have a vision of one's nationhood. You must have a vision as to where you wish your children to be, and then you assess your priorities accordingly.
We learn every day that governments give moneys to questionable enterprises. We learn every day that national governments refuse, for whatever reasons, to collect appropriate taxes from corporations that ought to be paying them. We learn that governments give moneys to their friends and to their political cronies. But on the other hand-and this is a serious point-we give very little in terms of money, time and concerted effort with regard to child poverty and poverty as a whole.
So I would say to the hon. member that perhaps she ought to change her vision as to where she wishes this nation to go. Yes, members on this side are concerned with regard to the deficit as are members on that side and I am sure are members to the left. But if you want to eradicate child poverty in this country, your view must change. You must have the political will. You must have the courage to say no to the corporate elite in this country who get off without paying appropriate taxes. You must say no to your political cronies wherever they may be and provide the appropriate money for child care. You must say no to those provincial governments who wish to extract money from the Government of Canada and then spend it elsewhere. That is what you must do.
I urge the hon. member to change the vision that she may have, that her party certainly has, in order to rectify and to put a priority with regard to child poverty and poverty as well.

I think you will find that there is agreement that while we will continue with our usual rotation of speakers, if one of the parties wishes to break up the 20-minute speech and 10-minute question and comment period they could do that by having a 10-minute speech and a five-minute question and comment period and take two of those. I would seek the unanimous consent of the House to allow that to occur for the rest of the day to enable the maximum number of speakers to have a chance to raise their voice on this most important issue.

This matter has not come to my attention since the hon. member has just raised it. Perhaps we could continue on with the speaking order that we have in place I could report to him very shortly in terms of whether or not that consensus can be given on behalf of our party.
In that case I recognize the hon. member for Vancouver East.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to limit my remarks so that others will have an opportunity to speak on this very important topic.
I am sure all members of the House were very moved, as I certainly was, at the last address from my leader, the hon. member or Oshawa, when he spoke so emotionally about the importance of us taking action together to eliminate child poverty in Canada. His approach was non-partisan and appealed to all parties and to all leaders across Canada because, of course, provinces have a very important role in this mission.
He appealed to the media. I could not agree with him more. The media must take a much greater responsibility to make the public aware that this is one of the most tragic aspects of life in Canada today. We do not want it just to be done at Christmas time. I think a lot of us talk
about the funds for children at Christmas and then we forget them the rest of the year.
Our leader spoke about the tragedy in the fact that one in four children in Canada are poor. This figure is not diminishing very quickly at all. He said that 151,000 children line up at food banks each month. From 1974 to 1986 we know that 86 per cent of the working poor families increased and this was an increase of about 19 per cent. Poverty for families is still in a very devastating situation and there is no question that we need con- | certed action from all of us.
Last year I had the honour to chair an interparliamentary committee which met as part of the Interparliamentary Union Conference in Hungary. We studied the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and made resolutions to the larger body.
I want to say that I was very moved by the representations from delegates from many different countries of the world who spoke of the situation of children. They spoke of children in many Third World countries who are dying of starvation and preventable disease, children who were being brain damaged and permanently disabled by malnutrition, children who were abandoned because of war and poverty and the movements of people in many countries, and the serious neglect that comes with poverty in every country of the world. The people we talked to from Third World countries could not understand how, in a country as affluent and well endowed as Canada with our rich resources and our low birth rate, we could have over a million children who are poor.
We know that in Third World countries one of the reasons they cannot make any headway, in fact they are going backward in trying to provide a floor of health and welfare services that would protect children, is because of the immense pressures of international debt, a debt which we should be doing something about. We do not have those kinds of restrictions. Yet we have children who are lining up at food banks every month.
Canada is a signatory to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. This week we actually signed the formal declaration that passed the UN. We have an obligation to act here in Canada. We must bring our standards up to recognize the right of every child to a standard of living adequate for the child's physical, mental, spiritual, moral and social development. That is
November 24, 1989

what we said we would do when we signed that agreement.
The motion that is before us today in the House asks us to seek to achieve the goal of eliminating poverty among Canadian children by the year 2000. I wish we could agree to take major steps in this direction during 1990. I, for one, am not satisfied to wait until the year 2000. If we were to delay action until the year 2000 we would have a whole generation of children who would continue to be victimized and damaged and who as adults would be unable to function adequately in society. The unending cycle of poverty from family to family would continue.
As my leader pointed out, the solution to poverty is to get more money into the households of poor families. He proposed several specific measures to reduce poverty which I would just like to summarize again.
He proposed that we should have action on the part of the federal government, something which could be done immediately, to raise the federal minimum wage which is the lowest in Canada, and that this minimum wage should be indexed so that it provides jobs at adequate incomes for poor families.
He proposed that family allowance and the child tax credit, the two federal programs that are targeted directly to families and to children, and particularly to low-income families, should be raised. I would propose that we consider raising this to 20 per cent in 1990.
He proposed reintroduction of effective and affordable quality child care programs.
He also proposed a national conference on the elimination of child poverty involving the provinces, municipalities, voluntary agencies, labour, chambers of commerce, and all people, including all federal departments that can make some impact on poverty in Canada. He proposed that this group meet annually, establish targets and timetables and in fact to act as an advocacy group and an ombudsman group to make sure we take practical and specific steps as quickly as possible to alleviate poverty for children in Canada.
The minister talked in vague terms about redistributing wealth and rationalized some of the credit programs which we do not believe have been very effective for
Supply
low-income families. He talked about increasing the amount of wealth in Canada. I want to say that children are being victimized now. They will not be victimized further because of the national debt in Canada. Children should not be sacrificed to the national debt.
If we were to put money now into satisfactory incomes for low-income families with children, we could have one million poor children over the next 10 years who would be adequately nourished, have adequate housing and child care and the opportunities to grow into mature adulthood. This would, in effect, result in one million adults and their families who would break the poverty cycle and who would become contributors to the tax system of Canada. Even in economic terms, we have to take action.
We need the political will to address this problem, and we need it on all sides of this House. Unfortunately, I must say that the policies carried out by this government have not addressed this issue, and I do not want to dwell on this today, but we must remember that the trade deal and the shifting of production south of the border is very hard for families. Changes to UI will restrict benefits for many low-income families. The national child care program has been indefinitely postponed. The clawback of family allowance and old age security benefits are a direct impact on low-income families.
The lack of monitoring of the Canada assistance cost-shared programs and the threats to cut shared programs with the provinces are also of great concern, not to mention the increasing impact of both the goods and services tax and the inflation that will hit low-income families as a result.
What can we all do together to really make some impact on poverty? First of all, we need to have major increases in family incomes. I would suggest that although there are many people who are poor, including single people and still many single older women, who we must not forget, that probably there is some justification to targeting a major income increase to families with young children.

I would be very pleased to finish my remarks very quickly, Mr. Speaker.
Not only do we need to increase incomes, we need to have affordable housing for low-income families. So much of their incomes goes to rent. We must have an affordable, good child care program across this country. Of course, we have to change policies in order to redistribute income.
I just want to say in closing that I hope we will all work, perhaps through the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare, as an all-party action group to sponsor a national conference on the elimination of child poverty, and to get on with the specific measures in the federal jurisdiction which we can take immediately to make some impact on this problem.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to express my appreciation for the opportunity to join in this debate. I wish also to congratulate my leader on his last speech in this body for bringing up a subject that I think this body tends to avoid or to steer around because we are all a bit ashamed of the figures concerning child poverty and the figures relating to poverty in this country.
I was pleased to see at the beginning of the debate how members seemed to adopt this issue as one that was rather non-partisan, we would all like to deal. I hope as a result of this debate the few examples of partisanship that did introduce themselves will be forgotten. I hope that ultimately the wording of the motion will be the thing that will be remembered by people in this House. Essentially, what this motion is asking us to do is to set as a priority the elimination in this country of child poverty by the year 2000. If there is anything we choose to remember about the Leader of the New Democratic Party and about this debate, it should be the challenge that he has thrown out to the House of Commons and to the people of Canada. This is a personal challenge that I think he has taken on, to eliminate this terrible child poverty that we experience in this country by a certain time period.
I do not think we could expect the Minister of National Health and Welfare to come back within the scope of
this debate and list a series of priorities which he would adopt under this motion. I certainly would have hoped for a commitment from the minister and perhaps from his parliamentary secretary that he would go out and take part in the structure suggested, such as a national conference on poverty, or perhaps by referring the issue to the health and welfare committee of this House. I hope that he will work to develop a series of programs that would ultimately result in achieving the challenge that the Leader of the New Democratic Party has set for us.
I do not want to go through the statistics that have already been enumerated by a number of the speakers in this debate. They are terrifying statistics especially, for those who experience the reality of poverty in their | day-to-day life. What struck me was one of those statistics which points out that in the industrialized countries of the world, Canada is the second worst in terms of child poverty. We are second only to the United States in how poorly we deal with this problem.
The member for Oshawa pointed out to us that there are other countries to which we can look as models and countries which seem to have established as a priority the elimination of child poverty. These are countries which are doing much better than we are. If there are these models around the globe, then at least we should be committing ourselves to look at these models to see how they do it, at least to examine their priorities and possibly try to match our priorities to theirs in terms of eliminating poverty.
The fact is hundreds of thousands of Canadian children go to bed hungry every single night of the year. Hundreds of thousands of children go to school every morning without an adequate breakfast and without a school lunch. They do not perform well in school as a result of the fact that they have a problem of poor nutrition. They suffer academically as a result and often cannot complete their schooling because of nutritional and other problems.
There are tens of thousands of children in this country who as a result of inadequate clothing, inadequate insulation in their homes and sometimes a lack of fuel altogether, suffer more than other children in this country from common diseases such as respiratory diseases and others which can be easily dealt with if they had proper clothing, shelter and fuel or the wherewithal to acquire those things. Unfortunately in Canada there
November 24, 1989

are tens of thousands of children and tens of thousands of families who do not have the wherewithal.
In large part the blame for that problem lies with we in this House, because of the things we do or neglect to do. It is because of the priorities that we establish or neglect that those children and their families are suffering in poverty.
There is a group in British Columbia called End Legislative Poverty. Poverty in this country is not an accident. It is not an accident of any individual. People who are poor are not necessarily lazy or incompetent. They are not necessarily people who cannot obtain the wherewithal to live normal lives. Poverty in this country is legislated. It is legislated through what we do in this House or what we omit to do in this House. We on all sides of this House are the people who are responsible for the problem of poverty in Canada.
I reject the suggestions made by one member opposite who would wish to blame a previous government for creating the debt problem here.
I recall the minister saying that one of the problems we have is that when the economy expands we are going to be able to look after the issue of poverty. On the other hand he is saying that when the economy goes down again those people are going to become poor again. We are going to leave those people subject to the variations in the economy. That does not make sense. We have to establish an absolute priority in this House that no Canadian is going to be pushed into poverty as a result of the variations in the economy. If any government has that policy, it does not belong in government. If any member has that policy, they do not belong in this House.
I look back on a statement made by Abraham Lincoln. He said, "This nation cannot exist half slave and half free". If he qualified that statement by saying, "except in bad economic times", we would never remember that President as a great liberator. In fact, his name would have been tarnished from that day to this.
Our object in this Parliament should be to follow the challenge that the Leader of the New Democratic Party has laid out for us, that is, to set as a goal for the year 2000 that no child in this country should be a poor child, that no family in this country should be a poor family.
Supply
This country is rich enough and we as a collective are wealthy enough to make sure that is the case. I think what simply remains for us to do is to set that goal for ourselves and to work hard to reach that goal. That can be done through the conference that our leader has suggested, as well as through establishing priorities through a committee of the House-whatever it takes. Let us, out of this debate, establish that as our goal.
I think we should put a banner up in the House outlining the goal to eliminate child poverty in this country by 2000. I think we should put other banners up showing how we perform as those figures go down. By my stars, if those figures do not go down, then we do not deserve to be re-elected as members of this House. Let us establish that goal. Let us set it up where we can see it. Let us challenge ourselves every single day to make sure that we accomplish it.
A part of the problem in this issue is the attitudes that we hold as a group. People in Canada think that those who are poor are all on welfare. As the gentleman who spoke previously pointed out, in fact the vast majority of people who are poor in this country work for a living, and they work hard. In some cases because they work at minimum wages, very low wages, they work at two jobs. In some cases, both heads of families work. So it is very difficult when you tell people that they should work in order to get out of poverty and they find themselves going deeper and deeper into poverty. While costs go up, while taxes go up, and while interest rates go up the fact is the minimum wage has stayed very low. The minimum wage in this country is not sufficient for hard working people to work themselves out of poverty. I applaud my leader for his suggestion to raise that minimum wage so that we can bring those people who work for a living out of poverty.
There is also the suggestion that poor people are all on welfare and that they do not pay their own way. Studies which have been carried out across this country, in particular at Dalhousie University in Nova Scotia, have analyzed the taxes paid by poor people. The results show that not only do they pay for their own programs, they pay more. They pay for other people as well, people who are not poor.
There is a serious problem with the way taxes are structured in this country. There are taxes that favour rich people and which are generous to them but which create a burden and an oppression on the poor. There

November 24, 1989
Supply
are many things that have to be done in order to eliminate the problem of poverty in this country.
I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, and I will tell the rest of the people in this House, the one thing that first needs to be done is the one thing that is called for in this motion. Members of Parliament unanimously have to establish as a goal the elimination of child poverty by the year 2000. We should establish that out of this motion making it a goal of this Parliament.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member whether he could give us some suggestions, since he says the government should introduce legislation. Does he have any suggestions about the kind of legislation the government should table in the House to deal with the problem of child poverty, and doesn't he think that one way to deal with poverty is to ensure that families have access to jobs? Is he prepared to acknowledge that the government-although of course it was not 100 per cent, since nobody is perfect-has made considerable progress, since the unemployment rate has declined from 11.6 per cent in September 1984 to 7.4 per cent in October this year, and the youth unemployment rate has declined from 18.2 to 11.3 per cent? Will the hon. member acknowledge that the government deserves some credit for introducing policies that promote job creation in this country?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the parliamentary secretary for her question. I would like to point out that many of the jobs that have been created since the recession of 1981-1982 are part-time jobs at very low rates of pay, in fact at minimum wages both in the provinces and nationally. As I pointed out in my speech, those people who are working at those minimum wages, in some cases at two jobs, simply cannot make the money to make ends meet, to feed their families, to get decent shelter, to put decent clothing on their children and to provide for decent education and medical care.
As a response to the question I just want to give the example of a woman in my riding who, as a result of a marriage breakdown, went on welfare. She felt humiliated by being on welfare. Her daughter had a chronic illness. Although welfare provided her with a less than
adequate income, fortunately, it provided her with free medical care, free dental care and with prescription drugs that her daughter desperately required.
When she tried to take training to go back to work to become a legal assistant she was disqualified from welfare because the course was one year long. She went anyway and was able to beat the system and take that course.
Then she went to work in a lawyer's office and she was paid at the minimum wage. She lost the right to those free medical, dental and prescription drug benefits. She ended up making less on the minimum wage than she made when she was on welfare. Her daughter's health was put into jeopardy as a result of that.
What we need is a system that addresses those kinds of obstructions to work and that raises the minimum wage so that people who are working can look after their children and are not forced to sacrifice the health and safety of their children simply by getting off welfare and going to work.
There are a lot of things that need to be done. We are the people who have the power to do it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to speak to the motion on child poverty.
On behalf of the Minister of National Health and Welfare I would also like to take this opportunity to thank the leader of the New Democratic Party on behalf of the poor childen in this country, for addressing their concerns in his last speech on an opposition day. It is an eloquent example of the hon. member's great sensitivity to the problems of the neediest in our society.
I sincerely hope that after he leaves Parliament, the hon. member will continue his active involvement in addressing the terrible problem of child poverty and especially, Mr.Speaker, the appalling increase in child sexual abuse.
November 24, 1989

I think that as a private citizen, the hon. member for Oshawa would be in an excellent position to increase Canadians' awareness of this very serious problem.
The family is our starting point in this world. It is the environment in which we grow up and it teaches us sharing and compassion.
Although we are aware of the problems facing families today, we must not forget that most families, whatever their structure or status, are responsible and take care of their family members and are proud to see them grow up and make their way in this world.
When I was growing up, Mr. Speaker, most of our families consisted of a father who worked outside the house and a mother who worked at home. We had strict discipline and felt secure in our family unit. However, as we approach the year 2000, the family is undergoing major changes and faces economic pressures and significant challenges.
In over 60 per cent of Canadian households, both spouses are in the labour force. Thus, most children live in an environment where their parents do double duty: Work outside and family responsibilities. Many of these children, who do not receive the same family support as I did when I was growing up, do not feel loved and wanted; they often feel as though they are in the way because when their mother comes home from work, she is pre-occupied and perhaps unfortunately does not have the time to give them all the attention they deserve.
Furthermore, one marriage in three ends in divorce or separation. Therefore, the probability that Canadian children will spend part of their childhood in a singleparent family increases every day.
These facts shape the daily reality of today's younger generation, and as decision-makers, we cannot escape them. Child poverty is also another reality for some Canadian families. One child in six is poor, as poverty is defined in Canada. This situation could jeopardize the development of some of tomorrow's adults and their chance to reach their full potential; we cannot be indifferent to it.
That is why the government has taken action to support the family. Without resting on our laurels, of course, we must be glad that child poverty has declined
Supply
since the Conservative Government took power. This improvement is due to the economic recovery of recent years, the lower unemployment rate which has benefited all families and social programs for the economic betterment of families. Economic priorities are the guarantee of our future prosperity.
In that respect I should mention the value of the refundable child tax credit which is designed to help low-and middle-income families and which has gone up by 50 per cent since 1984, from $367 to $565. Close to five million children stand to benefit from this measure this year. For that credit alone the federal government will issue cheques totalling about $2 million.
Aware of the tight financial situation of families with children, in November the government sends an advance part payment of the child tax credit to eligible households. Mr. Speaker, God knows the month is well chosen-just in time for Christmas! We also help support families through the monthly family allowances paid for each child under age 18.
This year, roughly 6.6 million children will be entitled to the allowance and the federal government's outlay will amount to about S2.6 billion. In the Province of Quebec alone, 1.6 million children receive the monthly allowance.
Mr. Speaker, I might point out that pursuant to specific Family Allowances Act criteria the provinces may choose the way to distribute the allowances. This enables them to give greater consideration to their own priorities. The Province of Quebec avails itself of this provision. For instance, Quebec youths aged 12 to 17 inclusive get a higher allowance than younger children. The amount of the allowance also increases according to the child's rank in the family.
We know for a fact that poverty is more prevalent among children of single-parent families. It is more difficult for a single parent to assume his or her economic and family responsibilities in a world where two parents generally look after the child. What is more, the economic situation of a single-parent family takes a turn for the worse when the marriage breaks up.
Anxious to help the provinces enforce support orders and family agreements, the federal government has created two services. The first uses federal data banks such as the unemployment insurance benefits central file

November 24, 1989
Supply
to keep track of parents who have defaulted in their financial obligations. The second service recuperates from the defaulter parent the amounts administered and paid out by the federal government such as tax refunds and public pension plan or unemploymewnt insurance benefits.
Although these services have been operative for only a few years, they report that the number of retraced parents and seized funds is on the increase. Single parent families are the first to benefit from these improvements. Thanks to the new GST, the tax system will be made more equitable through a number of integrated changes which will make it possible for low income families to receive tax credits. So, following the implementation of the new GST, families earning under $30,000 a year will be much better off.
The government has publicly commited itself to supporting families through social measures aimed at developing a day care network and at ending family violence. Let us not overlook the significance of the Canada Assistance Plan whose costs are equally shared by the Federal and Provincial Governments and whose purpose is to provide financial assistance to needy families. Let us not forget either the convention on the Rights of the Child which was proposed and adopted this week by the United Nations, more specifically on November 20. The purpose of this Convention is to set up modem international standards aimed at protecting the social, economic, political, religious, cultural and civil rights of children.
Mr. Speaker, in order to live up to these new international standards, we will have to amend our relevant legislation. In my humble opinion, I feel that in view of these rights, we will have to take steps to make sure that physically and sexually abused children are getting the help they need to overcome the trauma they have suffered. I am thoroughly convinced that as we near year 2000, the growth of this country will largely depend on our investments in our human resources, and this from childhood.
I have examined here only some of the steps the federal government has taken in its effort to eliminate poverty among young Canadian children. At the provincial level, non-government and community organizations play an essential role. I will mention for instance
the province of Quebec which has adopted a family policy dealing with several aspects of family life.
In conclusion, I should like to say that the family represents our main institution and our children the future of our society. I am 39 years old and childless which I consider a personal tragedy. For that reason, I love other people's children, and I just could not tolerate anybody hurting any of my nephews, nieces or any other children I know.
Within the next few months, Rix Rogers, a special advisor on sexually abused children, will submit a long awaited report. I wish to emphasize once more that I am determined to ensure that the federal government, together with the provinces, implements its recommendations, in order to deal once and for all in a fair fashion with the serious problem of child abuse.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for her comments, and I agree that a number of programs have been continued, that some improvements have been made in some cases, and that a few new but rather limited initiatives have been taken.
[English)
Here is the record as I understand it. There have been 31 tax increases during the last five years. There has been a goods and services tax proposed affecting disproportionately the poor. In spite of the comments that have been made to the contrary, we get no agreement from the poor on that.
There will be a goods and services tax that taxes sports such as ringette, hockey, bowling, private music lessons, books and other reading materials, many of those very important to children and poor children in particular, non credit college and university courses, and even the simple niceties of life such as candies and other treats, as well as certain health services such as psychological services and the services of psysiotherapists. There is also the content of the last budget which a lot of people called an anti-family budget; it claws back from seniors and it claws back from families. How have these helped? If one looks at the total context, how have these helped to reduce the three and one-half to five million poor in Canada, and the little over one million children, the almost one million families, many of them single parent familiesled primarily by women, and the over one million unattached adults, most of whom are women? How has it
November 24, 1989

reduced the food banks that we are told are of the order of 150 to 160 and the soup kitchens? How has it helped the unemployed who do not appear on the unemployment list because they have run out of benefits and lost hope, or the almost 25 per cent youth unemployment in Newfoundland?
If we look at these new initiatives that my hon. colleague speaks about in the total context, can she tell me honestly that the poor in this country are not as numerous and that they are better off than they used to be?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the present time, incredible demands are being made on the federal government, both in the area of health and welfare and the environment. The amounts of money required in these two areas alone are astronomical.
I hope hon. members don't think that the government is particularly happy to have to raise taxes in order to achieve a more equitable distribution of the tax base. But although much remains to be done, some progress has been made. I may mention that the number of Canadians living below the poverty line has declined by more than 549,000, which means 179,000 children, 61,000 senior citizens and 198,000 women are no longer living below the poverty line. It may not be spectacular, but it is a positive development.
Personal disposable income after taxes, Mr. Speaker, has risen by $1,400 per capita, in real terms, since September 1984. Of course these are statistics, and when in our ridings we see children and families who are poor, we wonder why they can't be part of the statistics. It is clear the government has some very serious problems with the deficit, and at the same time we have a very serious social problem that we must deal with.
Of course, the only way the government can do anything is through the tax base. And although we don't particularly like raising taxes, we have to if we are to make any attempt at dealing with the problems facing so many poor families in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased for the opportunity to speak to this important motion before the House today. The emphasis we in Canada place on our social programs and the intensity of our national belief in sharing and equity help make Canada the great country that it is. We take pride in the deep rooted tradition of caring for the less fortunate among us.
For these reasons, the issue of poverty is a distressing one for all Canadians; poverty in a country so richly endowed as Canada should not be happening. It is a matter of serious national concern. We are among the most concerned about those in our society least able to overcome poverty by their own efforts and we are speaking, of course, of those children who live in poverty.
It must be pointed out that there are clearly problems associated with the definition and measurement of poverty in Canada and with child poverty in particular. Thus, for example, the number of children cited in the motion as living in poverty cannot be accepted as an accurate picture of the real situation. That fact in no way diminishes the seriousness of child poverty nor the importance of seeking to reduce or eliminate it. The intent and spirit of the motion deserves the support of all members of this House.
It is an unfortunate fact that the welfare of children and the opportunities they have to life to a great extent depend upon the economic circumstances of their parents. Those children who are raised in poor families may veiy likely experience significant material deprivation. The lack of an adequate family income will very likely impose relative hardship on children in those families. Clearly, improving family income, raising the standard of living of low-income families is fundamental to reducing child poverty and eliminating the roadblocks to opportunities that it creates.
The best way the government can help raise many families out of their low-income situations is to ensure Canada has an economy that is operating at its potential. Canada needs to have a strong productive economy to generate the jobs and economic activity that translate into higher incomes and to finance our social network. In short, a key to reducing poverty among children is a strong economy.

November 24, 1989
Supply
The Conservative government has been working to build a dynamic and competitive economy that will raise standards of living and provide the means to sustain the valued programs that are part of the social fabric of this country. It has done so through an economic strategy introduced n 1984, which this government has been following ever since. There are two basic aspects to this economic plan: To ensure sound stewardship of national finances and to make fundamental changes to the economy so as to unshackle the private sector and promote competitiveness and innovation.
Over the past five years we have made substantial progress on these two fronts. The government's annual deficit has been reduced considerably below the levels of the 1984-85 period. We have also made and are continuing to make significant changes that improve the way the economy operates. By removing frictions and distortions, we are making the economy more productive. By improving productivity we are raising the living standards of Canadians and thus making headway in fighting poverty.
The actions we are taking are many and far-reaching: The Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, forward-looking trade initiatives with Europe and Pacific Rim countries, the deregulation of energy and transportations sectors, tax reform, privatization, new skills training for the labour force and a new competition policy are just a few.
These changes have contributed to a healthier, more confident private sector. They are part of the new foundation we are building for a stronger, more dynamic and prosperous economy in the next decade and beyond.
This plan is working. Over 1.5 million new jobs have been created in Canada over the past five years, unemployment rates have dropped in every region of the country and, more important, Canadians have benefited from these improvements. By helping to put in place and maintain a healthier economic environment, the government has laid the groundwork for social programs, lower levels of poverty and unemployment, and a more progressive distribution of after-tax income.
Over the past five years, we have taken a number of specific steps to help alleviate child poverty by increasing child benefits through the tax system to low-income families. For example, in the February 1986 budget we
introduced a three stage increase in child tax credits and a new supplement to the child tax credit. There is a prepayment now of two-thirds of the child tax credits to about 700,000 low income families that was also started in 1986.
In stage one of tax reform, we converted the child tax exemption to a credit in order to benefit low income Canadians. The federal sales tax was increased in the April 1989 budget. These increases represent a first step to the new refundable sales tax credit that will accompany sales tax reform. The Social Planning and Research Council of British Columbia has found many on income assistance who must use part of their food money to pay for rent, and estimates are that about 60 to 70 per cent of the household income of poor families is spent on shelter. As the minister has acknowledged, this contributes greatly to child poverty.
Under the Co-op Housing Program which is the only separate federal program available directly from the federal government to municipalities, we have only about 100 units available this year in Vancouver. As the minister knows, the cost of housing is escalating and the amount of affordable housing is diminishing greatly. This is really contributing to the stress on families and to poverty generally. I know the minister gave his overview
November 24, 1989

of government programs. Putting that aside, deal with this problem of the high cost of shelter for poor people?

Mr. Speaker, I very much appreciate the question from the hon. member, because that, in effect, is what I was trying to outline in the concluding portion of my remarks. These are some of the practical things I have been trying to do to expand, given the limitations on finances that we have, and in trying to use the resources that we have available in a better fashion.
The hon. member spoke of co-op housing. There was a discussion and agreement between the Co-operative Housing Foundation of Canada and the government some four years ago with respect to an experimental program with index-linked mortgages. That is the program that we have been applying over the last four years. It has another year to go under the agreed experimental program. One of the problems with that program was it anticipated that we could have a real interest rate of 4 per cent on ILM mortgages. But we have had a real interest rate of 5 per cent as opposed to 4 per cent. One of the ways to get that real interest rate down is to get more people investing in index-linked mortgages.
I have been going out to pension fund groups as a messenger on behalf of co-op housing and ILM mortgages to try to sell them on interest rate down to the 4 per cent level. For each 1 per cent of interest rate, the interest rate on an ILM mortgage drops, and we could increase the amount of co-op housing we produce by 20 per cent, and I have had some success.
As the hon. member knows, I was in Vancouver about two or three weeks ago and we opened a co-op housing project. This was in conjunction with the city of Vancouver which purchased the Killamey Gardens property comprising 227 units, an existing project which was about to be tom down and a condominium built in its place. In a co-operative effort with the city of Vancouver, the co-op housing movement and the federal government through the use of ILM mortgages, where we backed a $19 million ILM mortgage, we were able to save that property for co-operative housing. Those are the kinds of practical things we should be looking for and that we should be trying to do to assist in helping child poverty and in helping all poverty across this country.

There are many other things that we are trying to do in order to be innovative using the resources that we have available to expand the amount of housing for Canadians, whether it be for first-time home buyers or people spending vast sums of their income on housing who are not able to afford it, so that we can create more homes and put more people in them, still facing the realities of the existing federal fiscal situation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me this afternoon to be able to participate in this debate, a debate that was started off this morning in the name of the hon. member for Oshawa. It struck me this morning that not only the motion but the hon. member's speech probably summed up his career in this House and the contribution he has made to conscience in this country and the thought that so many of us must have in addressing problems like this.
There is no place in Canada that sees and suffers from poverty like Newfoundland and Labrador. Like all members but I regret perhaps more than some that in my own constituency I see it every time that I am home. We all must through our efforts, not only in terms of legislation but in terms of our consciousness, move to ensure that poverty is eradicated in this country now and forever. I was particularly taken by the comments made this morning by my colleague, the member for Cape Breton-East Richmond. They reflect so much the perception and reality in Atlantic Canada.
The hon. member for Oshawa reminded us that if there is anything we lack in this country, it is an awareness of the situation. It is an awareness that poverty is everywhere, that poverty is so destructive and so insipid. It is an awareness that we can, each in our own little way, do something about it. It is coming from that awareness that I want to speak this afternoon in the few brief minutes that I have about the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Yesterday afternoon I had the privilege of meeting with 21 students from the Upper Gullies Elementary School in Conception Bay South in my constituency. They were a representative group of 70 Grade 6 students who came to me with their principal, Mrs. Peckham, and a teacher, Mrs. Wells, and asked me to come to the House of Commons and say that Canada has co-sponsored and endorsed through the United Nations the

November 24, 1989
Supply
convention that deals with the rights of children and that Canada should be the first country to endorse that in its own legislature. I bring that message to you, Mr. Speaker. They gave me 70 letters. I have them here and I read them this morning. They talk primarily of two things, of ratification and of peace. Ratification is something that I will come back to.
Briefly the students see the lack of peace in this world as one of the greatest crises that children face. We know that children are the victims of political violence. We know that children are the victims of war. We know that children suffer most around the world as they are pawns and as they are left by the side as we carry on in our political differences and in the interests of some great principle that we seem to have. What these kids are saying to me and to all of us is summed up perhaps in a letter from Jennifer Anthony which says: "Why can't everyone just co-operate and work together? Why don't they just try it? The world would be a much better place if people would just try to work everything out without going to war".
I think all Canadians are proud of the role this country has played in the United Nations in having the UN endorse the convention. We co-sponsored it as everyone knows and I am sure that all members will agree that the letters they received from their constituents were encouraging that we move decisively, and we have done that. Now the question is for ratification. But I think it is important to recognize that the convention while we think of it as applying to others has some very important messages for Canada and for Canadians.
Article 6 for example gives recognition to the concept of survival and development. But that is just more than the essentials of life. That includes such things as growth monitoring, oral rehydration, breast feeding, immunization, disease control, and child spacing. Article 24 talks about health and nutrition; Article 26, on the right to benefit from social security; Article 27, on the right to an adequate standard of living including access to material assistance and support programs.
Clearly considering our role in the movement of this resolution through the UN gives us an extra responsibility in terms of ratification and also in terms of compliance. The convention is a very comprehensive and detailed instrument providing for a number of important rights for the child and quite specific obligations for states. Clearly the subject matter in this convention as it applies to Canada falls into provincial as well as shared jurisdiction. Clearly there must be a continued ongoing process of consultation with the provinces and the territories. I need not remind hon. members that the provinces have played a very substantial role in the development of our position on this and our co-sponsorship.
Ratification demands that this country have the legislation in place because once we have ratified it we have accepted it. This country, and I think all members would agree that our responsibility is to ensure that we do have the mechanisms in place, that we have the legislation and regulations in place so that compliance is not something that we cannot do. Compliance is something that we must be willing to do, and do in an active and constructive manner. The provinces again must be a substantial part of that contribution.
There will be a committee on the rights of the child put in place. It will provide constructive criticism in working with states to facilitate implementation and provisions of the convention. In a sense it will be a monitor.
As we all know, and as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has indicated, poverty is not just a problem in Canada. Poverty is a tragedy in this country, particularly for our children, there is no question. I cannot help but comment as we see the atrocities in El Salvador, as we look at the violence around the world that leaves children parentless, that leaves children homeless, that leaves children without the basic sustenance of life, that leaves children hopeless. I look at the situation on the horn of Africa, particularly as it pertains to Eritrea where fighting on behalf of Ethiopia there are children carrying weapons. We see it every day in the Middle East. We see it every day around the world.
When I speak to people outside of this place I try to remind them that what happens outside of this country directly pertains to their lives inside of this country, that the welfare of people around the world matters in a material way to the way that we live today and in the

future. I come back to the awareness problem. We must be aware of those needs, those concerns as we as a country play a leadership role not only in serving the needs of those around the world that need our help but also as a facilitator, as a mover toward peace, as a country that can lead this world into the future in a more sane and more humane way.
I am not normally prone to reading letters but there are three that I mentioned. One is very simple from Paul Martin:
Please pass a law immediately about the law of the child, not to use money to make weapons but to get shelter and clothes.
There is also a poem from a lady by the name of Nancy Carter which is only four lines:
Why do people fight when it only kills? Why do they kill when it only makes people sad? Why do people have war when it makes no sense? I pray each day no more war will come. God save us from the war.
If we can tell children around the world that they have a future, we in Canada will be able to tell our children as we move to their future that it, too, will be secure and that this country will lead the war in dealing with poverty and world security.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment the member for his very eloquent remarks.
I would like to ask him if he is aware that the Member of Parliament for Mission-Coquitlam has sponsored a private members' bill to establish a children's bill of rights that is designed, as I understand it, to conform to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.
I think it really relates to what he was saying and, having studied this question, I agree with him. It is important that Canada not only ratify the UN declaration but that we find a way of implementing it. It seems to me that this is one of the ways that we could.
I wonder, first, if he would consider supporting this private member's bill and perhaps even co-sponsoring it so that we could have it sponsored by people on all sides of the House. Then it would go forward as this motion has today in a non-partisan way so that there is consensus in working for the rights of children in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I confess not to being specifically aware of the private member's bill. It is my understanding that the government, as the minister mentioned this morning, supports the concept and is doing some work on it.
I would suggest, though, that because of the timing involved we should move and move quickly with any initiative like this. It is not an accident that the convention was signed this week. It commemorates 30 years of the declaration. As well, 10 years ago was the Year of the Child.
In terms of my co-sponsoring the bill, I have not yet seen it and no politician nor anybody else with any sense would agree to anything until seeing it. However, we recognize that there is some momentum there and a real consciousness. I am sure the hon. member got all sorts of letters supporting this process and Canada's involvement. I think that consciousness is something that we should build on.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the member for St. John's East for a very articulate statement of fact and support on behalf of the children of Canada. Really, it was a speech that I was anticipating. The only question that I have for the member is simply what are the numbers of children living in poverty in Canada. Does he have statistics for us?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not have a figure. Quite clearly, there have been numbers bandied about here today. Poverty is something that is more than money in the pocket. As I see it, poverty is lack of care, lack of shelter and lack of some sense of future. I see people every day who live on nothing, but who provide remarkably loving and secure homes for their children. These children have a future because they are taught that they have one.
The answer to the question may be that if there is one, it is too many. I think all of us, whether on this side of the House or on the other, work to make sure that there are none, because children in this country and children around the world have to be the future. We mark children from very early days. They are affected by their environment from the very beginning. The more secure that environment is, the more stable health care systems are and the more able children are to cope in the world, the better they are to be functional and to contribute to whatever country they live in.

If we have one child who is not getting that anywhere in the world, our work is not finished.
Hear, hear!
